From the oval shaped flower bed there rose perhaps a hundred stalks, spreading into heart shaped or tongue shaped leaves half way up and unfurling at the tip red or blue or yellow petals marked with spots of color raised upon the surface. <break time="0.8s" /> Out of the dim throat of each flower emerged a straight bar, rough with gold dust and slightly clubbed at the end, and the petals were voluminous enough to be stirred by the summer breeze. <break time="0.8s" /> When the petals moved, the red, blue, and yellow lights passed one over the other, staining an inch of the brown earth beneath with a spot of the most intricate color. <break time="0.8s" /> The light fell upon the smooth gray back of a pebble or the shell of a snail, or, falling into a raindrop, it expanded with such intense color that one expected the drop to burst. <break time="0.8s" /> Men and women walked past the flower bed with a curiously irregular movement, not unlike that of the white and blue butterflies that crossed the turf in zigzag flights from bed to bed. <break time="0.8s" /> A married couple with two children came by, the man strolling carelessly about six inches in front of the woman, who now and then turned her head to see that the children were not too far behind. <break time="0.8s" /> The man, whose name was Simon, kept this distance on purpose, though perhaps unconsciously, for he wanted to go on with his thoughts, which had been carried back fifteen years to this very garden.

Fifteen years ago he had come to Kew with Lily and had begged her to marry him, and as they sat by a lake, a dragonfly kept circling round and round them in the heat. <break time="0.8s" /> How clearly he could still see the dragonfly, and her shoe with the square silver buckle at the toe, moving impatiently while he spoke, so that he knew her answer without looking up at her face. <break time="0.8s" /> He had told himself that if the dragonfly settled on a leaf she would say Yes at once, but it went round and round and never settled anywhere, and Lily had not married him. <break time="0.8s" /> Turning to his wife at last, Simon asked her whether she ever thought of the past, and he confessed that he had been thinking of Lily, the woman he might have married. <break time="0.8s" /> Far from minding, Eleanor answered calmly that one always thought of the past in a garden where men and women lay under the trees, for they seemed to be the ghosts of ones own happiness. <break time="0.8s" /> For her part, she remembered six little girls sitting before their easels by a lake twenty years ago, painting the first red water lilies she had ever seen, when suddenly a kiss fell on the back of her neck. <break time="0.8s" /> It had been given, she said, by an old gray haired woman with a wart on her nose, and it was the mother of all her kisses all her life. <break time="0.8s" /> Come, Caroline, come, Hubert, Eleanor called, and the family walked on, four abreast, until they diminished in size among the trees and looked half transparent in the trembling sunlight and shade.
